title: Primary and Secondary Works
paragraphs: > Usage is > What is in vogue and use > Among the literate > From whom issue > The events of popular speech.
(Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 93)
> Primary or original works > Are those compositions > By men of sage wisdom > Whose consummate faculties stand unsullied > By the mire of turpitude.
(Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 95)
> Secondary works comprise four modes.
(Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 97)
> These four modes are: > Summarization, elaboration, > Synthesis of summarization and elaboration > And translation in conformity with the tradition of the receptor tongue.
(Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 98)
The explanations of these four verses are as follows:

(1) Given the fact that the events of popular speech draw on the use of language by the literate, what is called linguistic usage is the usage of the literate. This apart, this usage defines and informs the worldly usage, poetic usage and the normal, grammatical usage. Following the literate usage and simplifying the poetic usage and the worldly usage for the people at large to access it will go a long way in the development and protection of the language.
(2) The present work gave me the opportunity to engage myself in the protection and preservation of the Tamil language.
(3) When it comes to the meaning of verse 95 given above, a misinterpretation will give room for assumptions and questions like
Tolkāppiyam is the primary work. • It was composed by a person of consummate wisdom. • He was also the one of unblemished mind. • Will Tolkāppiyar go to describe himself in such terms?
Primary works are those that precede and that form the basis or the source of secondary works.
Dr Ilakkuvanar in his Study of Tolkāppiyam observes as follows:

> It is said that Tolkāppiyam is the earliest extant work in Tamil. No other work predating Tolkāppiyam has come to us. It does not mean that no work was written before Tolkāppiyam. Tolkāppiyam is a work of grammar. In any language, literature precedes grammar. Tamil is no exception to this. Here too grammatical works came to be written only after the advent of literary works. Tolkāppiyam was written after not only works of literature but also grammatical treatises, which is attested to by Tolkāppiyam itself. Therefore, Tolkāppiyam must be seen as the earliest extant work and not the first, primary work.
Even before we arrive at an answer to the question of whether Tolkāppiyam is the
primary text, there have come up false mythic accounts like,

Akattiyar was the teacher of Tolkāppiyar. Akattiyar was the one who wrote the first book in Tamil. Pāṇini had written a grammatical text in Sanskrit before Tolkāppiyar. Tolkāppiyar was the son of the Aryan sage Camatakkini. Camatakkini was the father of Paracurāmaṉ. Paracurāmaṉ and Rāmaṉ were contemporaries. Akattiyar belonged to the period of Rāmaṉ. Tolkāppiyar too belonged to the same period.

What is strange here is that Rāma’s age is fixed before 2000 BC. Pāṇini’s period was 350 BC. Had Tolkāppiyar lived after Pāṇini, Paṉampāraṉār in his prologue to Tolkāppiyam might not have described Tolkāppiyar as the one versed in Aintiram. He would have called him versed in Pāṇini’s treatise. As such, it is obvious that Tolkāppiyam preceded Pāṇini’s work.

Now, let’s come to the Tolkāppiyam verse referred to above. It does not speak of whether Tolkāppiyam is a primary text or not. On the other hand, it discusses the nature of secondary works. A secondary work implies that there must be a primary work. The verse in question just outlines the what and how of a primary work.
But some of our scholar-commentators tend to give the impression that the author of a primary work is God.
Not just that. Shouldn’t we realize the wily misdirection behind such assertions like Akattiyam is the primary work of the ancient era, and Tolkāppiyam is based on this work.

As I have shown earlier, we must ignore such things as to whether Tolkāppiyam is a primary work and whether the primary work was authored by God. And we must treat this and the following verses in Tolkāppiyam as describing primary and secondary works.
The verse
> viṉaiyiṉ nīṅki viḷaṅkiya aṟiviṉ > muṉaivaṉ kaṇṭatu mutal nūlākum
must read as
> viḷaṅkiya aṟiviṉ muṉaivaṉ kaṇṭatu > viṉaiyiṉ nīṅki mutal nūlākum
which means that men of consummate wisdom write what are called primary works, works that are faultless and that precede secondary works.
Verses 3 and 4 speak of the four kinds of secondary works: synthesis, elaboration, both synthesis and elaboration, and translation.
